newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown seen flat after 1997 budget approval.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown seen flat after 1997 budget approval.

text.p: The Czech crown was expected to remain flat on Monday after Friday's partial selloff when foreign parties squared long positions before the vote on the government's 1997 budget, dealers said.

The crown was trading ahead of the central bank's fixing on Monday at 27.414 to the dollar, 17.615 to the mark or 2.65 percent above parity with its mark/dollar basket, roughly the same as Friday's late close after the budget was approved.
The central bank fixing followed the market, as the Czech National Bank put the currency at 27.402/dollar, 17.611/mark or +2.67 percent above parity.

Pavel Bouc, a dealer at Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka (CSOB), said that with the 1997 budget out of the way, he thought the crown would ease slowly to a range between 2.3 to 2.5 percent above the basket through the Christmas holiday.
"All the fundamentals which are still coming from our economy -- this means the balance of trade deficit and so on -- they aren't the best," Bouc said.
"Also the extrapolations of some specialists are saying that we will have inflation of around nine or 9-1/2 percent again. I think all these factors are against the strength of the crown," he added.

Parliament approved the conservative government's fifth straight balanced budget plan on Friday, but the 1996 budget is expected to show a slight deficit of over one billion crowns because of lower-than-expected revenue collection.

Meanwhile, the current account deficit for 1996 is seen at around seven percen of gross domestic product, while some economists have said annual inflation, which has edged back under nine percent, will remain stubborn.
